Stripling
STRIP-ling
n. (a youth not yet full grown; Saul's word for David after Goliath fell)
From strip, in the sense of a long thin slip of wood, with the diminutive -ling — a stripling is a lad as slender as a strip. It renders Hebrew elem, a young man, used only twice in Scripture.

Biblical Definition

The word appears in the strangest possible place. Goliath is dead, David is walking back with the head in his hand, and Saul — who had armed him personally an hour earlier — turns to Abner and says, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is. A stripling: a slip of a lad, not a man yet. It is the third time the chapter has measured David that way. Saul had said, thou art not able to go against this Philistine, for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth; and the Philistine, when he looked about and saw him, disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance. Everyone in the story agrees on the assessment and everyone is wrong about what it means, because none of them heard the argument David made to Saul — the lion and the bear, thy servant slew both, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God. Paul writes the same principle to a young minister facing older men: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers — not, insist on your standing, but give them nothing to despise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a youth in the state of adolescence, or just passing from boyhood to manhood; a lad.

expand to see more

STRIPLING, n. A youth in the state of adolescence, or just passing from boyhood to manhood; a lad.

YOUTH, n. The part of life that succeeds to childhood; a young person; a young man.

DISDAIN, v.t. To think unworthy; to deem worthless; to scorn; to contemn.

RUDDY, a. Of a red color; of a lively flesh color, or the color of the human skin in high health.

EXAMPLE, n. A pattern; a copy; a model; that which is proposed to be imitated.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 17:56 — "And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is."

1 Samuel 17:33 — "And Saul said to David, Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth."

1 Samuel 17:42 — "And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance."

1 Timothy 4:12 — "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity."

Modern Corruption

Youth is flattered as a qualification in itself or dismissed as disqualifying; Scripture does neither — it tells the young man to be an example and tells the church not to despise him.

expand to see more

The church in the West has spent a generation treating youth as an asset to be marketed — younger leadership, younger music, a younger look — as though the calendar conferred insight. Scripture is unsentimental about this. It gives the office of elder its name from age, requires that a man not be a novice lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil, and commands the younger to submit themselves unto the elder. David, for all his courage, was not made king that afternoon; he went back to the sheep, and waited years, and refused twice to take the throne by force when it was within reach of his hand.

The opposite error is just as real, and Paul wrote against it. Let no man despise thy youth was addressed to a church, not only to Timothy, and the remedy Paul prescribes is not a demand for respect but a life: be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity. Six areas, all observable. Saul asked whose son the stripling was because a boy had just done what the whole army would not. The question a church should be asking about its young men is the same one — not how old is he, but what has he already done in the fields where nobody was watching.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew elem (H5958), a young man or stripling; naar (H5288), a youth or servant lad; Greek neotes (G3503), youth; kataphroneo (G2706), to despise.

expand to see more

Hebrew elem (H5958) — a stripling; used only twice, both times of David in this chapter.

Hebrew naar (H5288) — a boy, a lad, a servant; the word Saul and Goliath both use of him.

Greek neotes (G3503) — youth; what Timothy was told not to let men despise.

Greek kataphroneo (G2706) — to think down upon, to despise; the same verb used of despising the riches of God's goodness.

Greek tupos (G5179) — a pattern, an example; the remedy Paul gives for being despised.

Usage

"“Enquire thou whose son the stripling is” — asked with a giant's head in view."

"“thou art but a youth, and he a man of war” — the reasonable assessment."

"“Let no man despise thy youth” — and the six-part answer that follows it."
